99|protocolSection.descriptionModule.briefSummary: "Pain due to peripheral nerve lesion remains extremely difficult to treat and current treatments have onl moderate efficacy and/or side effects. The investigators have previously demonstrated the long term efficacy of Botulinum toxin type A (BTX-A) in a small group of patients with post-traumatic/postherpetic neuralgia and allodynia. The present study aims to a/ confirm the efficacy of repeated applications of BTX-A in a larger group of patients with peripheral neuropathic pain with or without allodynia(primary outcome) ; b/ evaluate its mechanisms of action ; c/analyse the predictors of response ;d/analyse whether the second injection is associated with a therapeutic gain. This will be a randomized placebo controlled study. A total of 30 patients will be randomized to receive either BTX-A (subcutaneous injection in the painful area) or placebo. Each injection will be repeated within at least 3 months depending on the duration of efficacy. Skin punch biopsies will be performed before and 1 month after BTX-A administration. The investigators postulate that this study will confirm the clinical efficacy and good safety of repeated administrations of BTX-A in the treatment of peripheral neuropathic pain."

42|toxin A in peripheral neuropathic pain (BOTNEP):
43|a randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial
44|Nadine Attal, Daniel C de Andrade, Frédéric Adam, Danièle Ranoux, Manoel J Teixeira, Ricardo Galhardoni, Irina Raicher, Nurcan Üçeyler,
45|Claudia Sommer, Didier Bouhassira
46|Summary
47|Background Data from previous studies suggest that botulinum toxin A has analgesic eff ects against peripheral
48|neuropathic pain, but the quality of the evidence is low. We aimed to assess the safety and effi cacy of repeated
49|administrations of botulinum toxin A in patients with neuropathic pain.
50|Methods We did a randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial at two outpatient clinics in France (Clinical Pain
51|Centre, Ambroise Paré Hospital, APHP, Boulogne-Billancourt, and Neurological Centre, Hôpital Dupuytren,
52|Limoges) and one in Brazil (Neurological Department, Hospital das Clínicas da FMUSP, São Paulo). Patients aged
53|18-85 years with peripheral neuropathic pain were randomly assigned (1:1) by block randomisation, according to a
54|centralised schedule, to receive two subcutaneous administrations of botulinum toxin A (up to 300 units) or placebo,
55|12 weeks apart. All patients and investigators were masked to treatment assignment. The primary outcome was the
56|effi cacy of botulinum toxin A versus placebo, measured as the change from baseline in self-reported mean weekly
57|pain intensity over the course of 24 weeks from the fi rst administration. The primary effi cacy analysis was a mixed-
58|model repeated-measures analysis in the intention-to-treat population. This trial is registered with ClinicalTrials.gov,
59|NCT01251211.
60|Findings Between Oct 2, 2010, and Aug 2, 2013, 152 patients were enrolled, of whom 68 were randomly assigned
61|(34 per group), and 66 (37 [56%] men) were included in the primary analysis (34 in the botulinum toxin A group and
62|32 in the placebo group). Botulinum toxin A reduced pain intensity over 24 weeks compared with placebo (adjusted
63|eff ect estimate -0·77, 95% CI -0·95 to -0·59; p<0·0001). Pain on injection was the only adverse eff ect reported, and
64|occurred in 19 (56%) participants in the botulinum toxin A group and 17 (53%) of those in the placebo group (p=1·0).
65|Severe pain was experienced by ten (29%) participants in the botulinum toxin A group and 11 (34%) in the placebo
66|group (p=0·8).
67|Interpretation Two administrations of botulinum toxin A, each of which comprised several injections, have a sustained
68|analgesic eff ect against peripheral neuropathic pain. Several factors, such as the presence of allodynia and a limited
69|thermal defi cit, may be useful in predicting treatment response and should be investigated further.
70|Funding Institut National de la Santé et de la Recherche Médicale (INSERM) and Fondation CNP (France).
71|Introduction
72|Botulinum toxin type A is widely used to treat muscle
73|hyperactivity,1 on the basis of its ability to inhibit synaptic
74|exocytosis and, therefore, to disable neural transmission.
75|In the past decade, fi ndings from several experimental
76|studies in animals and healthy people have suggested
77|that botulinum toxin A might have analgesic activity
78|independent of its eff ect on muscle tone,2,3 which has led
79|to the suggestion of new indications for the drug in
80|analgesia, particularly for chronic migraine.4 Findings
81|from prospective studies on dystonia,5 bladder dys-
82|function,6 and chronic migraine4 have shown repeated
83|administrations of botulinum toxin A to be safe, but the
84|safety and effi cacy of repeated administrations of this
85|drug for neuropathic pain have not yet been investigated.
86|Neuropathic pain is a debilitating chronic pain disorder
87|and an unmet medical need.7 Most drugs used for the
88|management of neuropathic pain have dose-limiting
89|adverse eff ects,8 and eff ective drugs without systemic
90|side-eff ects are urgently needed. Published data3,8 suggest
91|that botulinum toxin A has analgesic eff ects against
92|peripheral neuropathic pain. However, the quality of the
93|evidence is low because it comes mostly from small pilot
94|trials. Findings from one unpublished multicentre study
95|of 117 patients with postherpetic neuralgia9 showed no
96|eff ect of botulinum toxin A compared with placebo on
97|pain intensity from pain diaries (primary outcome), but
98|in view of the inclusion criteria (minimal duration of
99|pain required for inclusion was only 3 months), some
100|patients might have recovered spontaneously. No study
101|has assessed the effi cacy of repeated administrations of
102|botulinum toxin A for the treatment of neuropathic pain.
103|Furthermore, the phenotypic profi les of the patients who
104|respond to the drug have yet to be characterised.
105|We did a double-blind, randomised, placebo-controlled
106|trial to assess the safety and effi cacy of two subcutaneous

6|Methods
7|Study design and participants
8|We did an investigator-initiated, randomised, double-
9|blind, placebo-controlled, parallel-group clinical trial at
10|three outpatient clinics: two in France (Clinical Pain
11|Centre, Ambroise Paré Hospital, APHP, Boulogne-
12|Billancourt, and Neurological Centre, Hôpital Dupuytren,
13|Limoges) and one in Brazil (Neurological Department,
14|Hospital das Clínicas da FMUSP, São Paulo).
15|We enrolled consecutive patients with neuropathic pain,
16|based on a score of at least four out of ten on the DN4
17|(douleur neuropathique en 4 questions) questionnaire,10
18|who met the criteria for probable or defi nite neuropathic
19|pain according to the International Association for the
20|Study of Pain.11 Patients aged 18-85 years who had daily
21|pain for at least 6 months attributable to a peripheral nerve
22|lesion, who were able to understand the questionnaires,
23|and who could comply with the protocol visits were eligible
24|for inclusion. We excluded patients with a contraindication
25|(eg, infection at injection site) or hypersensitivity to
26|botulinum toxin A; disorders of the neuromuscular
27|junction (eg, myasthenia); coagulation disorders; previous
28|use of botulinum toxin; use of drugs acting on neuro-
29|muscular junctions, topical drugs (eg, capsaicin or
30|lidocaine), or anaesthetic blocks; progressive neuropathy;
31|major psychiatric disorders; facial pain (potential
32|unmasking); pain limited to the sole of the foot (potentially
33|greater adverse eff ects); an area of pain exceeding 240 cm2
34|(corresponding to the cutoff limit for botulinum toxin A
35|use in this study); or a mean pain intensity of less than
36|four out of ten on the numerical rating scale of the Brief
37|Pain Inventory. A full list of exclusion criteria is provided
38|in the appendix (p 2). Concomitant analgesic treatments
39|were authorised if they had been used at a stable dose for at
40|least 4 weeks before enrolment and were used throughout
41|the study.
42|This trial was approved by the competent authorities
43|and the relevant research ethics committees in France
44|and Brazil. All patients provided written informed
45|consent before inclusion.

51|Evidence before this study
52|We used a recent meta-analysis and systematic review that we
53|had coordinated to compile evidence regarding the effi cacy of
54|treatments for neuropathic pain, including previous pilot
55|studies of botulinum toxin A treatment. This meta-analysis
56|provided accurate up-to-date evidence about the safety and
57|effi cacy of the drugs recommended for neuropathic pain. We
58|identifi ed further reports specifi cally relating to botulinum toxin
59|type A published since this meta-analysis by searching PubMed
60|on Sept 30, 2015, with the Medical Subject Heading search
61|terms "neuropathic pain", "randomised controlled trial", and
62|"botulinum toxin" for relevant articles written in English
63|published since 2014. We identifi ed two additional randomised
64|controlled trials that met our quality criteria, but these studies
65|focused specifi cally on trigeminal neuralgia, which is outside the
66|scope of this study. The existing evidence supports the use of
67|tricyclic antidepressants; serotonin-norepinephrine reuptake
68|inhibitor antidepressants; pregabalin; gabapentin (including the
69|extended-release formulation) and gabapentin enacarbil;
70|tramadol; strong opioids; and, for topical applications, lidocaine
71|patches and high-concentration capsaicin patches for the
72|treatment of peripheral neuropathic pain. However, fi ndings
73|from our recent meta-analysis showed that these treatments,
74|although more eff ective than placebo, were generally only
75|modestly effi cacious, because the numbers needed to treat for
76|effi cacy (based on 50% pain relief) ranged from 3·6 to 10·6. For
77|botulinum toxin A, the available evidence from four published
78|single-centre randomised controlled trials (for peripheral
79|neuropathic pain) suggested effi cacy, with a low number needed
80|to treat of 1·9, whereas in one larger scale multicentre
81|unpublished study, this treatment was ineff ective. However,
82|most of the trials yielding a signifi cant reduction in pain have
83|been judged to constitute only low-grade evidence. These
84|studies had several limitations and were single-centre studies,
85|which might account for the reported low numbers needed to
86|treat, because small trials generally tend to overestimate effi cacy.
87|Furthermore, none of the studies used several administrations
88|of botulinum toxin A or aimed to identify responder profi les.
89|Added value of this study
90|This study is, to our knowledge, the fi rst randomised,
91|placebo-controlled multicentre clinical trial of repeated
92|administrations of botulinum toxin A in patients with
93|neuropathic pain to be reported. Two administrations of
94|botulinum toxin A injected subcutaneously (up to 300 units)
95|were effi cacious and safe for treatment of peripheral
96|neuropathic pain. This treatment is at least as eff ective as
97|existing treatments for the disorder, and its effi cacy was
98|enhanced by a second administration. This treatment was safer
99|than systemic treatment for neuropathic pain, as shown by an
100|absence of systemic side-eff ects. Furthermore, participants with
101|allodynia displayed the best responses to botulinum toxin A.
102|Implications of all the available evidence
103|Findings from this study, together with data from previous
104|studies, support the clinical relevance of botulinum toxin type A
105|for the treatment of peripheral neuropathic pain. Further
106|research should expand these fi ndings in larger and less
107|selected groups of patients.

26|Statistical analysis
27|In a pilot study with a similar endpoint,3 we noted a mean
28|diff erence in pain intensity between botulinum toxin A
29|and placebo of 1·5 units (SD 1·5). Since the selection of
30|participants was less stringent in this study-ie, not as
31|many exclusion criteria were used-we assumed that the
32|mean diff erence in pain intensity between the two
33|treatment groups in our study would be smaller (about
34|1·0 unit). Assuming a similar SD, we calculated that a
35|sample size of 30 participants per group would be needed
36|for 80% power, to detect such a diff erence in a two-sample
37|two-tailed t test with a type I error of 0·05. Taking into
38|account a 10% dropout rate, we estimated that we would
39|need to include 66 participants in total.
40|The effi cacy analyses for the primary outcome and for
41|all but one secondary outcomes included all randomly
42|assigned participants (intention-to-treat population)
43|and used a last-observation-carried-forward (LOCF)
44|imputation. Analysis of the therapeutic gain of the
45|second injection (a secondary endpoint) included all
46|randomly assigned participants who received two
47|administrations of the treatment (as-treated analysis,

75|In this randomised, placebo-controlled, three-centre trial
76|in patients with peripheral neuropathic pain, a series of
77|two botulinum toxin A administrations signifi cantly
78|reduced pain intensity over 24 weeks compared with
79|placebo and was safe and generally well tolerated. The

81|painful area of skin, as in real-life treatment. Repeated

83|deleterious eff ect on sensation. Furthermore, the
84|analgesic effi cacy of botulinum toxin A was enhanced by
85|a second administration 12 weeks after the fi rst; almost a
86|quarter of participants who displayed little improvement

8|Our fi ndings provide insight into the factors predictive
9|of favourable response to botulinum toxin A. We found
10|that allodynia and limited thermal defi cit at baseline
11|were associated with a better response to botulinum
12|toxin A; however, in our study population, the prevalence
13|of thermal defi cits was greater in participants without
14|allodynia than in those with allodynia. This particular
15|sensory profi le, characterised by preserved small-fi bre
16|function and hyperalgesia, has been described as irritable
17|nociceptors, and has been suggested to be related mostly
18|to nociceptor sensitisation, ectopic discharges, and
19|central sensitisation.23,24 These data suggest that
20|botulinum toxin A is more eff ective in patients who have
21|nociceptive input preservation. This fi nding seems to be
22|corroborated by fi ndings from skin punch biopsies that
23|show that baseline preservation of intraepidermal nerve
24|fi bres on the painful side was associated with a better
25|response to botulinum toxin A. However, these results
26|should be interpreted with caution because intra-
27|epidermal fi bres are not necessarily nociceptive aff erents,
28|and skin punch biopsy data could not be normalised to
29|the contralateral (ie, non-painful) side.
30|The identifi ed analgesic eff ects of botulinum toxin A
31|were not associated with changes in the total protein
32|concentrations of substance P or CGRP in skin punch
33|biopsy specimens. Although we cannot ascertain whether
34|total protein concentrations corresponded to neuro-
35|peptides released from nerve terminals, these data suggest
36|that the mechanisms of action of botulinum toxin A are
37|primarily unrelated to neurogenic infl am mation. We
38|postulate that the analgesic eff ects of botulinum toxin A
39|are predominantly related to central mecha nisms of pain
40|transmission, at least in those patients with chronic pain
41|disorders. In animals, botulinum toxin A inhibits central
42|nociceptor trans duction25,26 and central neurotransmitter
43|release.27,28 This central eff ect of botulinum toxin A might
44|relate to retrograde transport of the drug along the nerve
45|by axonal traffi cking mechanisms similar to those
46|involved in the transport of other pathogen-related
47|proteins.29 The fact that the eff ects of botulinum toxin A
48|were enhanced in participants with preserved nociceptive
49|input in our study is compatible with this hypothesis,
50|since nociceptive fi bres must be present for botulinum
51|toxin A to be transported and transcytosed in the CNS.
52|However, we cannot rule out that peripheral mechanisms
53|were also involved in the reported eff ects of botulinum
54|toxin A on paroxysmal pain, allodynia, and hyperalgesia,
55|because evidence suggests that these symptoms might be
56|sustained by a combination of peripheral and central
57|mechanisms.23,24,30 More specifi cally, we found that
58|botulinum toxin A alleviated mechanical allodynia and
59|hyperalgesia. These data are consistent with fi ndings
60|from an experimental study26 in healthy participants in
61|which botulinum toxin A decreased sensitivity to noxious
62|mechanical pain. These eff ects might be caused by the
63|ability of botulinum toxin A to reduce the proportion of
64|neurons expressing slowly adapting mechanically gated
65|currents, which is linked to mechanonociception.26

18|Several potential limitations of our study need
19|consideration. One is the moderate sample size; however,
20|our sample met statistical expectations for the primary
21|endpoint, we used several robust statistical models, and
22|we obtained positive results for the primary outcome and
23|several secondary outcomes. Our sample was also highly
24|selected; therefore, the present data should be further
25|investigated in larger settings with fewer exclusion
26|criteria. We used the LOCF method to impute for missing
27|data, which can overestimate effi cacy;31 however, this
28|method is a widespread method of imputation, especially
29|in neuro pathic pain clinical trials,8 and few data were
30|missing in the present study (appendix p 14).
31|Furthermore, fi ndings from a post-hoc sensitivity
32|analysis showed that the LOCF results were similar to
33|those of three other imputation methods. Finally, there
34|was risk of unmasking during the study period because
35|of the eff ects of subcutaneous botulinum toxin A on skin
36|appearance, specifi cally wrinkles or colour. We did not
37|photograph our participants' skin during the study, but
38|photographs of a woman who participated in this trial
39|and was treated after the trial with subcutaneous
40|botulinum toxin A for peripheral neuro pathic pain with
41|the same method and doses as in the present study show
42|no skin modifi cation (appendix p 15). Patients with facial
43|pain were excluded from our study, because the eff ects of
44|botulinum toxin on fi ne facial features would probably
45|contribute to unmasking; neither the patients nor the
46|investigators reported recognising the treatment because
47|of skin modifi cations.
48|In summary, our study shows the safety and effi cacy of
49|repeated administrations of botulinum toxin A in a group
50|of patients with peripheral neuropathic pain of diff erent
51|causes. The treatment was particularly effi cacious in
52|participants with preserved nociceptive input, as shown
53|by the presence of allodynia and minimal thermal defi cits.
54|These results highlight the relevance of a therapeutic
55|approach aiming to use treatments on the basis of clinical
56|phenotypes rather than the cause of pain.23,24,32-34

5|Inclusion criteria
6|Patients presenting all the following criteria were included in the study:
7|1) Men or women aged 18 to 85 years.
8|2) Spontaneous pain with a mean intensity over the last 24 hours of at least 4/10 on a 10-point numerical
9|rating scale (Brief Pain Inventory).
10|3) Pain of at least six months' duration.
11|4) "Pure" or predominant neuropathic pain (no other pain or only negligible associated pain), defined
12|according to the DN4 questionnaire (Bouhassira et al., 2005) and the criteria proposed by IASP (2008,
13|2011).
14|5) Pain related to mononeuropathy or stable polyneuropathy (posttraumatic, post-surgical, postherpetic,
15|mononeuritis in the context of a stabilized systemic disease, polyneuropathy linked to diabetes,
16|idiopathic polyneuropathy, systemic disease) confirmed by clinical examination and/or an appropriate
17|electrophysiological examination (EMG).
18|6) Patient mastering the French language and capable of understanding the study methodology and the
19|questionnaires.
20|7) Written informed consent obtained for participation in the study.
21|8) Painful zone limited to an area no greater than 240 cm2 and suitable for treatment administration.

4|Skin punch biopsy
5|
6|Consenting patients (n = 55) underwent two 3 mm skin punch biopsies before and four weeks after injection, as
7|described elsewhere (Lauria et al. 2005). Measurements were carried out in the area of maximal pain in all cases
8|and on the control side in 33 consenting patients from one site (Ambroise Paré hospital, Boulogne) : the latter
9|corresponded to the homologous contralateral area or to the adjacent area of normal sensitivity in patients with
10|polyneuropathy (e.g. the thigh). As the control side was not evaluated in all patients and given the variability of
11|body sites in which skin punch biopsy was conducted, we did not use normalised IENFD values.
12|Measurements were analysed blindly in the laboratory in Wurzburg (Germany):
13|1) In half the sample (n = 55), the density of intra-epidermal nerve fibres (IENFD) (in fibres/mm) was measured
14|before injection, according to internationally accepted quantification rules (Lauria et al 2005);
15|2) The other half of the sample (n = 50, 5 samples could not be analysed) was flash-frozen in liquid nitrogen and
16|stored at -80°C, as previously described (Kennedy et al 2000) before further processing for protein analysis of
17|substance P (SP) and calcitonin gene-related peptide (CGRP) immunostaining, using an enzyme linked
18|immunoassay (ELISA) (Substance P EIA Kit, Cayman Chemical Item Number 583751, detection level 8 pg/ml;
19|CGRP SPI bio A05481, detection level 5 pg/ml) respectively.

5|Therapeutic gain associated with the second injection of BTX-A or placebo
6|
7|Therapeutic gains (TGs) due to the second injection were determined by comparison with the results of the first
8|injection for the primary outcome (weekly self reported average pain intensity from pain diaries on the numerical
9|pain scale of the Brief Pain Inventory).
10|TGs were calculated according to the following formula : weekly pain scores TG variable, difference variant:
11|TGdiff = (Sj - BL2) - (Si - BL1), with Si being the scores that immediately follow the first injection, Sj the scores
12|that immediately follow the second injection, BL1 the first injection baseline score, and BL2 the second injection
13|baseline score (versus the last measurement before the 2nd injection).
14|Repeated-measurement models for the W13-W24 period made it possible to calculate gains in the form of least
15|square means (LSMs), that are mean TGs adjusted for the week (time) variable. The BL1 score (baseline at W0)
16|was not included in these models as it is already part of the formula for TGs.
17|All models analysing repeated measurements were obtained by the SAS MIXED procedure with the patient as
18|the subject, and restricted maximum likelihood (REML) was used to estimate the covariance parameters of the
19|models.

5|Methods and baseline values for quantitative sensory testing
6|
7|
8|Quantitative sensory testing was performed in 59 consenting patients at baseline, week 12 and week 24
9|using the same technique in subjects comfortably installed in a bed, in a quiet room, at a constant temperature
10|(22°C), by a single experienced investigator (one per site). The protocol was conducted according to recent
11|recommendations and prior pharmacological studies conducted by the Ambroise Paré group (Backonja et al
12|2013). We did not use the German Research Network Protocol on Neuropathic Pain (DFNS) (Rolke et al 2006)
13|because not all centers participating in our study were certified for this protocol and because it does not include
14|measurements of suprathreshold mechanical punctate/thermal stimuli. Testing order was randomised and the
15|assessments made included dynamic mechanical allodynia and mechanical and thermal (warm then cold)
16|psychophysical testing. Before the start of the experimental session, a series of thermal test stimuli were
17|administered to the volar surface of the hand, to enable the subject to get used to the testing procedure. Testing
18|was conducted on the area of maximal pain, with comparison with the homologous contralateral area where
19|possible, or with the adjacent area of normal sensitivity in patients with polyneuropathy (e.g. the thigh).
20|
21|Mechanical sensations and pain
22|
23|The intensity of brush-induced (dynamic) mechanical allodynia was assessed by stroking the skin
24|gently with a brush (3 times) (Somedic, Sweden). Stimulus detection and pain thresholds for mechanical stimuli
25|were assessed with calibrated von Frey hairs (0.06 to 300 g) (Somedic, Sweden). Care was taken to avoid
26|stroking the skin and to apply only one pressure stimulus. The subjects were instructed to close their eyes during
27|the procedure. The filaments were applied (at least twice) during a two-second period, with increasing and then
28|decreasing pressure. Detection thresholds were defined as the lowest pressure perceived by the subject, and pain
29|thresholds were defined as the lowest pressure considered to be painful. The force required to bend the filaments
30|was then converted into log units. After determining the mechanical pain threshold, suprathreshold stimuli were
31|applied in a pseudorandom order, using selected von Frey filaments. After each stimulus, the subjects were
32|asked to quantify pain intensity on a 100 mm visual analogue scale (VAS; from 0: no pain to 100: maximal pain).
33|If a VAS score of 80 or more was reported for a certain intensity, no stronger stimuli were applied. In such cases,
34|the same VAS score was assigned to all higher stimuli, facilitating the analysis of cumulative group data. This
35|method made it possible to plot mean stimulus/response curves for pain intensity as a function of graded
36|nociceptive mechanical stimuli.
37|
38|Thermal sensations and pain
39|
40|Thermal sensations were assessed with a thermotest (Somedic AB, Stockholm, Sweden), using the
41|Marstock method (Fruhstorfer et al., 1996). A contact thermode of Peltier elements measuring 2.5 x 5 cm was
42|applied to glabrous skin. A baseline temperature of 31.6°C and a thermal rate change of 1°C/s were used.
43|Thresholds were measured according to the method of limits previously described by Fruhstorfer et al. (1996):
44|briefly, increasing or decreasing temperatures were applied; for each stimulus the subject was instructed to press
45|a button that reversed the thermal stimulation, as soon as he or she detected the sensation of cold or warm
46|(detection threshold) or as soon as the stimulation became painful (pain threshold). All thresholds were
47|calculated as the means of three successive determinations. An interstimulus interval of 6 to 8 s was used when
48|testing perception thresholds whereas intervals of 15 to 20 s were used for heat pain thresholds and of 20 to 30 s
49|for cold pain thresholds. The maximum and minimum temperatures were set at 50°C and 5°C, to prevent tissue
50|damage.
51|
52|After determining pain thresholds, a series of suprathreshold thermal stimuli (5-50°C) were applied in a
53|pseudorandom order, as previously described (Hansson and Lindblom 1992). Each stimulus lasted 2 s and its
54|intensity increased or decreased in steps of 2°C for heat stimuli and 2.5°C for cold stimuli. We left an interval of
55|at least 1 minute between successive stimuli to prevent sensitisation. After each stimulus, the volunteers were
56|asked to rate pain intensity on a VAS. Subjects were informed that they could stop the stimulus at any time. If a
57|VAS score of 80 or more was reported with a certain intensity, no stronger stimuli were applied. In such cases,
58|the same VAS score was assigned to all stronger stimuli, to facilitate the analysis of cumulative group data. This
59|method made it possible to plot mean stimulus/response curves for pain intensity against graded thermal stimuli.
60|The same method was used for intensity-response curves for non-noxious cooling and warming.

5|The Neuropathic Pain Symptom Inventory
6|
7|The Neuropathic Pain Symptom Inventory (NPSI) is a validated questionnaire for neuropathic pain assessment
8|(Bouhassira et al. 2004). This questionnaire rates the intensity of five neuropathic dimensions (symptom
9|combinations) during the last 24 hours (burning, deep pain, paroxysmal pain, allodynia/hyperalgesia,
10|paresthesia/dysesthesia) on an 11-point (0-10) numerical scale. The presence and severity of the dimension
11|"allodynia/hyperalgesia" on the NPSI has been correlated to allodynia or hyperalgesia by quantitative sensory
12|testing (QST) (Attal et al. 2008).

13|thermal stimuli by (difference ≥ 2S) than on the control side (Backonja et al. 2013). These criteria were chosen
14|because of the large variability of pain thresholds and the lack of normative data for pain in response to
15|suprathreshold stimulation in healthy subjects (Backonja et al. 2013). Based on these criteria,
16|allodynia/hyperalgesia was detected in 29 patients (n = 59). Patients with allodynia/hyperalgesia had, on average,
17|smaller warm (p = 0.001), cold (p = 0.007) and mechanical deficits (p = 0.03) than patients without
18|allodynia/hyperalgesia.

7|LOCF as a method of imputation
8|
9|LOCF is one of the different methods of imputation that can be applied to datasets containing few missing data.
10|In the present study, out of 1650 data points for weekly pain (primary outcome) (66 x 25 records) only 131
11|(7.9 %) were missing, and out of 396 data points (66 x 6 visits), 29 (7.3 %) were missing. Because they were
12|more prevalent at the end of the 24 weeks period mostly due to dropouts (time effect, Friedman test: p<0.0001)
13|and more prevalent in the placebo group (2-sample Wilcoxon test: p=0.043) the missing pattern was identified as
14|Missing at Random (MAR). No baseline effect on the missingness was detected, thereby ruling out a Missing
15|Not at Random (MNAR) pattern.
